title: K-9 Saxon, Oxyglobin & the Saxon Award | Veterinary HBOC History
description: Documented 2002 real-world case of Fresno Police K-9 Saxon, Oxyglobin emergency use and the later Saxon Award, with source-linked veterinary HBOC context.
eyebrow: Historical Real-World Evidence · Working K-9 · Oxyglobin
heading: K-9 Saxon: Oxyglobin, survival and the legacy of the Saxon Award
lead: A critically injured police K-9 survived catastrophic line-of-duty trauma. The case was documented in Biopure's 2002 Annual Report, and Saxon's name later became part of Fresno Police Department policy through the Saxon Award.

sections.heading: The documented case
paragraphs: On 22 August 2002, Fresno Police Department K-9 Officer Saxon was shot at point-blank range during a line-of-duty incident. The Biopure Annual Report describes life-threatening injuries including lung injury, two broken legs and extensive trauma to his left side.

In a letter dated 26 November 2002 and reproduced in the report, Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer wrote that conversations with veterinarian Dr. Roger Gfeller left no doubt, in their view, about the pivotal role Oxyglobin played in saving Saxon's life. This is a historical company-published record and should be read as such, not as a controlled clinical trial.

sections.heading: The legacy became official
paragraphs: Saxon's story did not end with recovery. Fresno Police Department policy later established the Saxon Award in his honor, identifying him as the first Fresno Police Service Animal to be seriously injured in the line of duty on 22 August 2002.
The award recognizes a police service animal seriously injured in the performance of duty by unlawful force that could have resulted in death.

sections.heading: Why this case matters
paragraphs: Saxon is a documented historical example of a veterinary hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier being used in a real emergency involving a working dog. The case is relevant to the history of Oxyglobin, HBOC development and the broader concept of supporting oxygen delivery when conventional red-cell oxygen-carrying capacity is compromised.
For BHOC Veterinary, this case is historical context, not evidence of BHOC efficacy. It shows that oxygen-carrying therapeutics were used in real veterinary emergency care more than two decades ago.
